front: Policy vs standard vs procedure vs guideline
back:
Policy: high-level management statement of intent; mandatory (e.g., AUP, information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management)
Standard: mandatory, specific requirement that supports a policy (e.g., password, access control, physical security, encryption)
Procedure: mandatory step-by-step instructions (e.g., change management, onboarding/offboarding, playbooks)
Guideline: recommended, non-mandatory advice
comptiaNote: Only guidelines are optional. "All laptops use AES-256 full-disk encryption" is a standard, not a policy. A playbook is a procedure.

back:
Owner: senior business leader accountable for the data; sets classification, approves access, defines protection requirements
Custodian/steward: implements and maintains the controls the owner defines (backups, permissions, storage, day-to-day handling)
comptiaNote: Accountability stays with the owner; the custodian does the hands-on work. IT is usually the custodian, not the owner.

back:
Controller: decides why and how personal data is processed (purpose and means); accountable to regulators and data subjects
Processor: processes personal data on the controller's behalf and under its instructions (e.g., a payroll provider or cloud email-marketing platform)
comptiaNote: The company that collects the data for its own purposes is normally the controller, even when a vendor stores and processes all of it.

back:
Centralized: one central body makes and enforces security decisions for the whole organization → consistency and standardization; slower, less local fit
Decentralized: business units or regions make their own decisions within broad direction → agility and local fit; risk of inconsistency and gaps

Boards: top-level oversight; set direction and risk appetite, hold executives accountable
Committees: subgroups with a focused remit (e.g., audit committee, security steering committee)
Government entities: create laws/regulations and can oversee or examine organizations
Centralized/decentralized: where decision authority sits

Regulatory
Legal
Industry
Local/regional
National
Global
→ Policies must satisfy every jurisdiction and sector requirement that applies (e.g., a state privacy law, a national regulation, GDPR for EU data subjects, PCI DSS for card data)
comptiaNote: PCI DSS is an industry standard enforced mainly by contract with the card brands, not by a government law.

front: Monitoring and revision of governance documents
back:
Review on a schedule (e.g., annually) AND when triggered by: new laws/regulations, audit findings, incidents, new technology, business changes (e.g., hybrid work, cloud migration)
Revisions are approved, versioned, and re-communicated to staff
comptiaNote: An outdated policy is a governance gap even if it was correct when written.

back:
Defines what users may and may not do with the organization's systems, networks, data, and devices
Typical content: business-use rules, prohibited activities (unapproved software, illegal or offensive content), limits on personal use, monitoring notice, consequences of violations
Usually signed at onboarding and re-acknowledged periodically
comptiaNote: The AUP is often signed as a step of onboarding: the signed document is the AUP, the checklist that collects the signature is the onboarding procedure.

front: BC vs DR vs IR policy
back:
Business continuity: keep critical business functions running during and after a disruption (manual workarounds, priorities, alternate staffing)
Disaster recovery: restore IT systems, data, and infrastructure after a disaster (backups, alternate sites, recovery order)
Incident response: how security incidents are detected, reported, and handled, and who has authority to act
comptiaNote: BC = the business keeps operating; DR = the technology comes back. DR is usually treated as part of the broader continuity effort.

front: SDLC policy vs change management policy
back:
SDLC policy: requires security throughout the software lifecycle (requirements, design, secure coding, code review, testing, deployment, maintenance, retirement)
Change management policy: requires that changes to production systems are requested, impact-assessed, approved, tested, scheduled, and documented, with a backout plan

Onboarding: provision accounts with least privilege, sign the AUP and NDA, complete security awareness training, issue badge and equipment
Offboarding: formal HR-to-IT trigger, disable accounts on or before the last day, revoke badges, tokens, keys, and VPN access, recover devices and data, transfer file and mailbox ownership
comptiaNote: Accounts left enabled after someone leaves point to a failed offboarding procedure, a common audit finding.

back:
Password: minimum length, complexity or passphrases, reuse history, lockout threshold, hashed storage
Access control: least privilege, access model (e.g., RBAC), access review frequency, MFA requirements
Physical security: badge access, visitor logs and escorts, cameras, locked server rooms
Encryption: approved algorithms and key lengths (e.g., AES-256, TLS 1.2+), key management
comptiaNote: A standard is mandatory and specific ('must' plus a value); it supports a policy. 'Should' or 'consider' signals a guideline.

back:
Top-level security policy approved by senior management
States security objectives, scope, roles and responsibilities, and authority to enforce
Other policies, standards, and procedures derive from and support it
Reviewed on a schedule and when laws, threats, or the business change

SLE = AV × EF
AV = asset value
EF = exposure factor (percentage of the asset lost in one event)
Example: $200,000 × 40% = $80,000
comptiaNote: EF is the portion of value lost per event, not a probability. SLE is the cost of ONE occurrence.

back:
ALE = SLE × ARO
ARO = expected occurrences per year
Once every 5 years → ARO 0.2
Twice a year → ARO 2
Example: $80,000 × 0.2 = $16,000 per year
comptiaNote: Trap: "once every 4 years" is ARO 0.25, not 4. A control is cost-justified when (ALE before − ALE after) exceeds the control's annual cost.

back:
Qualitative: relative ratings of likelihood and impact (low/medium/high, heat map, risk matrix); fast but subjective
Quantitative: monetary and numeric values (AV, EF, SLE, ARO, ALE); objective but needs reliable data
Both combine likelihood/probability with impact

Appetite: the broad amount and type of risk the organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives (strategic, set by leadership)
Tolerance: the acceptable variance from that appetite for a specific risk or objective before action is required
comptiaNote: Study materials word these differently. Exam clues: 'willing to take on risk to pursue goals' = appetite; 'acceptable variance/deviation' = tolerance. The risk threshold in the risk register is the level that triggers a response.

front: Risk appetite: expansionary vs conservative vs neutral
back:
Expansionary: willing to accept more risk to pursue growth and innovation
Conservative: risk-averse; prefers lower risk even if it means missed opportunities
Neutral: balanced; weighs risk and reward evenly

Identified risks with description, likelihood, impact and score
Risk owner: person accountable for managing that risk
KRIs (key risk indicators): metrics that signal rising exposure (e.g., count of unpatched critical vulnerabilities)
Risk threshold: level at which the risk requires action or escalation
Planned response and status
comptiaNote: KRI ≠ KPI: a KRI warns that risk is increasing; a KPI measures performance against a goal.

back:
Transfer: shift the financial impact to a third party (cyber insurance, contract)
Accept: acknowledge and live with the risk (formalized as an exemption or exception)
Avoid: stop or never start the risky activity
Mitigate: apply controls to reduce likelihood or impact
comptiaNote: Transfer moves the financial impact, not the accountability. Residual risk is what remains after mitigation.

back:
Both are formal, documented, approved forms of risk ACCEPTANCE (listed under 'Accept' in 5.2)
Common framing:
Exception: approved deviation from a policy or control for a specific case, usually time-bound and periodically reviewed
Exemption: broader release from having to meet a requirement
comptiaNote: SY0-701 does not define the difference, and sources draw the line differently. What the exam tests: both map to the "accept" strategy.

back:
RTO (recovery time objective): maximum acceptable time to restore a system or process after a disruption → drives recovery speed
RPO (recovery point objective): maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time back to the last good copy → drives backup/replication frequency
comptiaNote: RPO of 1 hour means backups or replication must occur at least hourly. Both are set in the BIA.

back:
MTTR (mean time to repair): average time to fix a failed component and return it to service; lower is better
MTBF (mean time between failures): average operating time between failures of a repairable component; higher is better (reliability)
comptiaNote: If MTTR is longer than the RTO, the recovery design cannot meet the BIA requirement.

back:
Ad hoc: performed when needed, triggered by an event (new threat, incident, acquisition)
Recurring: repeated on a fixed schedule (e.g., annually, quarterly)
One-time: for a single project or decision, not repeated
Continuous: ongoing, often automated, near real-time evaluation

First step of risk management: find and describe risks before analyzing them
Inputs: asset inventory, threat intelligence, vulnerability scans, penetration tests, audit findings, incident history, interviews and workshops with business owners
Output: each risk (asset + threat + vulnerability) recorded in the risk register

Communicating risk status to decision makers and stakeholders
Audience: board, executives, risk owners, auditors and regulators
Content: top risks and scores, KRI trends, threshold breaches, treatment status, accepted risks and exceptions
Purpose: informed decisions, accountability, alignment with risk appetite

Likelihood: rating of how likely a risk is to occur (e.g., rare, possible, almost certain)
Probability: numeric chance of occurrence (e.g., 0.25, or 25% in a year); ARO expresses frequency per year
Impact: magnitude of harm if it occurs (financial, operational, reputational, legal)
Risk combines likelihood/probability with impact
comptiaNote: The terms are often used interchangeably; when contrasted, likelihood is the qualitative term and probability the quantitative one.

back:
Identifies critical business functions, their dependencies, and the impact of disruption over time
Sets recovery priorities and targets: RTO and RPO
Uses reliability data such as MTTR and MTBF to check whether targets are realistic
Feeds business continuity and disaster recovery planning
comptiaNote: RTO and RPO are targets the BIA sets; MTTR and MTBF are measured metrics. A BIA assesses impact; it does not reduce risk by itself.

back:
MOU (memorandum of understanding): informal statement of shared intent and goals; generally not legally binding
MOA (memorandum of agreement): more formal; documents the specific responsibilities each party agrees to

MSA (master service agreement): umbrella contract with general terms for all future work (payment, liability, IP, confidentiality)
SOW/WO (statement of work / work order): one specific project or task under the MSA: scope, deliverables, timeline, cost
comptiaNote: Typical pattern: one MSA, many SOWs.

back:
SLA (service-level agreement): measurable service commitments (uptime, response time) and penalties if missed
BPA (business partners agreement): terms between partners: responsibilities, profit/loss sharing, decision-making
NDA (non-disclosure agreement): obligation to keep shared confidential information private

Penetration testing (only with vendor permission and agreed rules of engagement)
Right-to-audit clause: contractual right to audit the vendor's controls
Evidence of internal audits: vendor shares its own audit results
Independent assessments: third-party reports (e.g., SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 certification)
Supply chain analysis: risk from the vendor's own suppliers, components and locations
comptiaNote: Independent third-party evidence gives stronger assurance than self-reported questionnaires or the vendor's internal audits.

back:
Due diligence: verify security posture, finances, reputation and compliance before signing
Conflict of interest: a personal or financial tie that could bias selection → disclose and recuse
Vendor monitoring: ongoing review after onboarding (SLA performance, incidents, reassessment)
Questionnaires: structured, self-reported security assessments
Rules of engagement: agreed boundaries for interaction and testing (scope, timing, contacts, permitted actions)

Right-to-audit: contract term letting the customer (or its chosen auditor) inspect the vendor's controls and records; must be negotiated into the contract
Independent assessment: a third party already evaluated the vendor (e.g., SOC 2 Type II report, ISO 27001 certification); customer reviews the report instead of auditing
comptiaNote: When the scenario says the customer lacks staff or access to audit the vendor itself, an independent assessment report is usually the expected answer.

back:
Strength: cheap, scalable, standardized way to collect security information from many vendors
Weakness: answers are self-reported and unverified
Fix: validate key answers with evidence (internal audit results, independent reports, right-to-audit, testing)

front: Supply chain analysis: what does it examine?
back:
The vendor's own suppliers and sub-contractors (fourth parties)
Origin of hardware components and firmware (counterfeit or tampered parts)
Software dependencies and third-party libraries
Geographic and geopolitical exposure of suppliers
Single points of failure in the supply path

Written authorization from the system owner (the vendor, for vendor systems)
Scope: in-scope and out-of-scope systems
Timing: dates and allowed testing windows
Permitted and prohibited techniques
Points of contact and escalation path
Handling of sensitive data found during testing
comptiaNote: A right-to-audit clause is not permission to attack vendor systems; active testing still needs agreed rules of engagement.

back:
1. Selection: NDA before sharing sensitive data, due diligence, conflict-of-interest checks
2. Assessment: questionnaires, evidence, independent reports, testing
3. Contract: agreements (MSA, SOW, SLA) with right-to-audit and security terms
4. Monitoring: ongoing performance and risk review, periodic reassessment
5. Offboarding: revoke access, return or destroy data

Due diligence: investigating and understanding risks and obligations (research, assessment, ongoing verification) → "knowing"
Due care: acting on that knowledge by implementing and maintaining reasonable protections → "doing"
comptiaNote: Failing to exercise due care is what exposes an organization to negligence claims.

back:
Fines
Sanctions
Reputational damage
Loss of license
Contractual impacts (penalties, termination, loss of the ability to process cards)

Reporting: internal (to management, board) vs external (to regulators, customers, partners)
Monitoring: due diligence/care; attestation and acknowledgement; internal and external; automation (continuous control checks, compliance dashboards)
comptiaNote: Attestation = a formal statement that something is true (e.g., an officer attests controls are in place). Acknowledgement = a person confirms they received and understand something (e.g., signing the AUP).

front: Data subject and right to be forgotten
back:
Data subject: the identifiable person the personal data is about
Right to be forgotten (GDPR right to erasure): the subject can request deletion of their personal data; the organization must comply unless an exception applies (e.g., a legal obligation to retain it)
comptiaNote: The right is not absolute: legally required records (e.g., tax invoices) can be kept, but only for that purpose and period.

back:
Data inventory: catalog of what data exists, where it lives, its classification, owner and who processes it
Data retention: keep data only as long as legally or business required, then dispose of it securely
Ownership: who is accountable for the data's use and protection
Legal implications: local/regional, national, global

Controller: decides why and how personal data is processed; accountable for compliance
Processor: processes personal data only on the controller's behalf and instructions (e.g., cloud or payroll provider)
comptiaNote: Classic trap: storing or hosting the data does not make a provider the controller; whoever decides the purpose is the controller.

back:
Internal: the organization checks itself (compliance team, internal audit, self-assessments, automated control checks)
External: outside parties check it (regulators, independent auditors, assessors such as a PCI QSA)
comptiaNote: Do not confuse monitoring (checking compliance) with reporting (communicating it to an internal or external audience).

back:
Local/regional: state or province laws (e.g., California CCPA/CPRA)
National: country-wide laws (e.g., US HIPAA for health data)
Global: laws with cross-border reach (e.g., GDPR covers organizations anywhere that offer goods or services to people in the EU)
Several levels can apply to the same organization at once
comptiaNote: GDPR is EU law; it is the usual 'global' example because it applies to organizations outside the EU that handle EU residents' data.

front: Data retention: too short vs too long
back:
Too short: violates legal or regulatory retention requirements, or destroys data under legal hold
Too long: larger impact if breached, more data exposed in legal discovery, conflicts with privacy rules such as storage limitation
Goal: a documented schedule per data type, then secure disposal

front: Known vs partially known vs unknown environment
back:
Known: testers get full information (diagrams, source code, credentials)
Partially known: testers get some information (e.g., IP ranges, a user account)
Unknown: testers start with no internal information, like an outside attacker
comptiaNote: CompTIA uses these names instead of white box, gray box and black box.

back:
Passive: gather information without interacting with the target's systems (OSINT, public records, social media, job postings, archived pages)
Active: interact directly with target systems (port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing); can be detected and logged

front: Penetration testing: physical, offensive, defensive, integrated
back:
Physical: test locks, badges, tailgating, facility controls
Offensive: attack the environment to find weaknesses (red team)
Defensive: detect and respond to the attacks (blue team)
Integrated: offense and defense work together and share findings (purple team)
comptiaNote: The 701 objectives use offensive/defensive/integrated rather than red/blue/purple.

front: Internal vs external audits and assessments
back:
Internal: compliance checks, audit committee oversight, self-assessments
External: regulatory audits, examinations, assessments, independent third-party audits
Attestation: a formal written opinion that controls meet a stated standard
comptiaNote: When stakeholders reject reports produced by the organization's own staff, the answer is an independent third-party audit.

back:
A formal written statement that claims about controls are accurate, usually an independent auditor's signed opinion on management's assertions
The audit is the process; the attestation is the signed result
Example: a SOC 2 report issued by an independent CPA firm
comptiaNote: If a question asks for the formal signed statement customers or partners can rely on, the answer is attestation, not assessment.

back:
Compliance: internal checks that the organization follows its policies, laws and contracts
Audit committee: board group that oversees internal audit, so auditors stay independent of the managers they audit
Self-assessment: staff evaluate their own controls (e.g., questionnaires, control reviews); cheap and frequent but not independent
comptiaNote: Internal audit keeps its independence by reporting to the audit committee, not to the CIO or CISO.

front: Physical penetration testing: what does it test?
back:
Whether people and facility controls stop unauthorized physical access
Examples: tailgating, badge cloning, picking or bypassing locks, posing as a contractor, planting a device on the network
Needs written authorization and agreed rules of engagement, like any other penetration test

front: Anomalous behavior: risky vs unexpected vs unintentional
back:
Risky: actions that bypass or ignore security and put systems or data at risk (disabling security tools, installing unapproved software, sharing credentials)
Unexpected: departure from a user's normal pattern (unusual hours, location, or resources accessed)
Unintentional: honest mistakes (wrong email recipient, misconfiguration, accidental click)

Development: assess needs and risks, set objectives, build content per audience
Execution: deliver training and phishing campaigns (recognizing a phishing attempt, responding to reported suspicious messages)
Reporting and monitoring: initial (baseline) and recurring (trends over time)
Use results to revise the program

Policy/handbooks
Situational awareness
Insider threat
Password management
Removable media and cables
Social engineering
Operational security
Hybrid/remote work environments
comptiaNote: "Cables" is there on purpose: malicious USB charging cables can carry implants, just like found USB drives.

front: Recognizing a phishing attempt: key indicators
back:
Urgency or threats ("account disabled in 2 hours")
Sender, reply-to or link domain that does not match the claimed sender (check by hovering)
Lookalike domains (e.g., a zero instead of the letter o)
Unexpected attachments or requests for credentials, payment or gift cards
Generic greeting, unusual tone or writing errors
comptiaNote: Logos and correct names are easy to fake; they never prove an email is legitimate.

back:
User: report with the report button; do not click, reply or forward
Security: analyze headers, links and attachments (sandbox)
If malicious: remove every delivered copy, block sender, domain and URLs
Find who clicked; reset those credentials and check those endpoints
Give the reporter feedback to encourage future reports

Situational awareness: notice what is happening around you (shoulder surfers, tailgaters, strangers without badges, unattended devices)
OPSEC: avoid leaking sensitive details through everyday activity (social media posts, whiteboards in photos, talking about projects in public)

front: Insider threat: warning signs to train users on
back:
Accessing data or systems unrelated to the job
Trying to bypass security controls or asking for extra privileges
Copying large amounts of data, especially before leaving the company
Strong grudges, unexplained wealth, unusual working hours without a business reason
Report concerns through the official, confidential channel
comptiaNote: An insider already has legitimate access, so perimeter controls do not stop them; trained coworkers are an important detection layer.

back:
Connect through the company VPN; avoid untrusted public Wi-Fi
Lock the screen when away; use a privacy screen in public
Keep work and personal devices and accounts separate
Use only approved storage, printing and collaboration tools
Watch for shoulder surfing and confidential calls in public spaces

Training explains the rules users must follow: acceptable use policy, data handling, password and remote work rules
The employee handbook collects these rules in one place
Users sign an acknowledgement at hire and after major changes
The acknowledgement shows users were told the rules; behavior metrics show whether training works
